title: 2026-10-28_Kobalos_Malware_Investigation_937
description: You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential Kobalos malware infection in a high-performance computing (HPC) environment. Kobalos is a complex, multiplatform malware that targets HPC clusters and other high-profile systems. It grants remote access to the file system, provides the ability to spawn terminal sessions, and allows proxying connections to other Kobalos-infected servers. Your goal is to identify and mitigate the threat.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential Kobalos malware infection in a high-performance computing (HPC) environment. Kobalos is a complex, multiplatform malware that targets HPC clusters and other high-profile systems. It grants remote access to the file system, provides the ability to spawn terminal sessions, and allows proxying connections to other Kobalos-infected servers. Your goal is to identify and mitigate the threat.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: Access the target host via SSH using the following credentials: Username: cyrano, Password: cyrano.
levels.local_content: Access the target host via SSH using the following credentials: Username: cyrano, Password: cyrano.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: While monitoring the target host, you notice unusual network activity. Investigate the running services on the target host to identify the suspicious service named 'payload-transfer.service'.
levels.solution: Use the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all running services. The suspicious service is named 'payload-transfer.service'.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Investigate the running services to identify any that seem out of place or unfamiliar.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all running services.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The suspicious service is not explicitly named here to encourage thorough investigation.

levels.title: Persistence Discovery
levels.content: Now that you have identified a suspicious service, determine how it is automatically started after a system reboot. Investigate the persistence mechanisms used by the malware and identify the enabled service named 'payload-transfer.service'.
levels.solution: Use the command `systemctl list-unit-files | grep payload-transfer` to check if the service is enabled to start at boot. The enabled service is named 'payload-transfer.service'.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Investigate systemd services, cron jobs, or other scheduled tasks that might be responsible for starting the suspicious service.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `systemctl list-unit-files | grep payload-transfer` to check if the service is enabled to start at boot.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The persistence mechanism involves a systemd service related to the suspicious activity.

levels.title: C2 Communication Discovery (Port)
levels.content: The suspicious service appears to be communicating with an external command-and-control (C2) server. Determine which network port is used for this communication.
levels.solution: Use the command `ss -tulnp | grep payload-transfer` to identify the network port used by the suspicious service.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Investigate network connections to identify the port used by the suspicious service.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Use the command `ss -tulnp | grep payload-transfer` to identify the network port used by the suspicious service.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The C2 port number is a four-digit number that you need to discover through your investigation.
